items.sentence_raw: According to the latest figures, the majority of the world's population is now bilingual or multilingual, having grown up speaking two or more languages.
In the past, such children were considered to be at a disadvantage compared with their monolingual peers.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says in the past bilingual children were *'considered to be at a disadvantage'*, but now researchers have identified *'several clear benefits'*. This shows attitudes changed from negative to positive. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Over the past few decades, however, technological advances have allowed researchers to look more deeply at how bilingualism interacts with and changes the cognitive and neurological systems, thereby identifying several clear benefits of being bilingual.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says in the past bilingual children were *'considered to be at a disadvantage'*, but now researchers have identified *'several clear benefits'*. This shows attitudes changed from negative to positive. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Research shows that when a bilingual person uses one language, the other is active at the same time.
When we hear a word, we don't hear the entire word all at once: the sounds arrive in sequential order.
items.explain: Q39: The question asks about the process of identifying heard words — paragraph B explains that sounds arrive *'in sequential order'* and the brain *'begins to guess what that word might be'* before it finishes. This describes exactly how people identify words. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Long before the word is finished, the brain's language system begins to guess what that word might be.
items.explain: Q39: The question asks about the process of identifying heard words — paragraph B explains that sounds arrive *'in sequential order'* and the brain *'begins to guess what that word might be'* before it finishes. This describes exactly how people identify words. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: If you hear 'can', you will likely activate words like 'candy' and 'candle' as well, at least during the earlier stages of word recognition.
For bilingual people, this activation is not limited to a single language; auditory input activates corresponding words regardless of the language to which they belong.
Some of the most compelling evidence for this phenomenon, called 'language co-activation', comes from studying eye movements.
items.explain: Q28: The passage directly names this phenomenon — *'this phenomenon, called 'language co-activation''* — where both languages are active at the same time. The question asks for the mechanism's name, and the passage gives it exactly. So the answer is **language co-activation**.

items.sentence_raw: A Russian-English bilingual asked to 'pick up a marker' from a set of objects would look more at a stamp than someone who doesn't know Russian, because the Russian word for 'stamp', marka, sounds like the English word he or she heard, 'marker'.
items.explain: Q27: The question asks what researchers observed in Russian-English bilinguals — the passage says they studied *'eye movements'* when people looked at objects. The example shows a bilingual person looked more at a stamp because the Russian word *'marka'* sounds like *'marker'*. So the answer is **eye movements**.

items.sentence_raw: In cases like this, language co-activation occurs because what the listener hears could map onto words in either language.
Having to deal with this persistent linguistic competition can result in difficulties, however.
For instance, knowing more than one language can cause speakers to name pictures more slowly, and can increase 'tip-of-the-tongue states', when you can almost, but not quite, bring a word to mind.
items.explain:
Q34: The question says bilinguals name images faster — but the passage says knowing more than one language *'can cause speakers to name pictures more slowly'*. **'More slowly'** is the opposite of **'faster'**. So the answer is **NO**.

Q40: The question asks about negative consequences — paragraph C mentions that bilingualism *'can cause speakers to name pictures more slowly'* and increases *'tip-of-the-tongue states'*. These are clear disadvantages of being bilingual. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: As a result, the constant juggling of two languages creates a need to control how much a person accesses a language at any given time.
For this reason, bilingual people often perform better on tasks that require conflict management.
items.explain: Q30: The question says bilinguals handle tasks involving a certain skill better — the passage explains they *'perform better on tasks that require conflict management'*. **'Conflict management'** is the exact skill named, connecting directly to handling conflicting information like in the Stroop Task. So the answer is **conflict management**.

items.sentence_raw: In the classic Stroop Task, people see a word and are asked to name the colour of the word's font.
items.explain: Q29: The question describes a test about naming colours — the passage introduces *'the classic Stroop Task'* where people name the colour of a word's font. The test name matches the description perfectly. So the answer is **Stroop Task**.

items.sentence_raw: When the colour and the word match (i.e., the word 'red' printed in red), people correctly name the colour more quickly than when the colour and the word don't match (i.e., the word 'red' printed in blue).
This occurs because the word itself ('red') and its font colour (blue) conflict.
Bilingual people often excel at tasks such as this, which tap into the ability to ignore competing perceptual information and focus on the relevant aspects of the input.

Bilinguals are also better at switching between two tasks; for example, when bilinguals have to switch from categorizing objects by colour (red or green) to categorizing them by shape (circle or triangle), they do so more quickly than monolingual people, reflecting better cognitive control when having to make rapid changes of strategy.
items.explain: Q31: The question asks what bilinguals have superior when switching tasks — the passage says they switch faster, *'reflecting better cognitive control'*. **'Cognitive control'** is the advantage named when making rapid strategy changes. So the answer is **cognitive control**.

items.sentence_raw: It also seems that the neurological roots of the bilingual advantage extend to brain areas more traditionally associated with sensory processing.
When monolingual and bilingual adolescents listen to simple speech sounds without any intervening background noise, they show highly similar brain stem responses.
items.explain: Q35: The question says bilinguals process sounds more efficiently *'in all situations'* — but the passage says without background noise, responses are *'highly similar'*. The advantage only appears *'in the presence of background noise'*. ***'In all situations' is wrong*** because it includes quiet conditions. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: When researchers play the same sound to both groups in the presence of background noise, however, the bilingual listeners' neural response is considerably larger, reflecting better encoding of the sound's fundamental frequency, a feature of sound closely related to pitch perception.

Q37: The question asks about a non-verbal auditory input — paragraph D describes how bilingual brains respond differently to *'simple speech sounds'* with background noise, which is a type of sound processing. This matches the question's focus on brain response to sound. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Such improvements in cognitive and sensory processing may help a bilingual person to process information in the environment, and help explain why bilingual adults acquire a third language better than monolingual adults master a second language.
This advantage may be rooted in the skill of focussing on information about the new language while reducing interference from the languages they already know.
Research also indicates that bilingual experience may help to keep the cognitive mechanisms sharp by recruiting alternate brain networks to compensate for those that become damaged during aging.
Older bilinguals enjoy improved memory relative to monolingual people, which can lead to real-world health benefits.

In a study of over 200 patients with Alzheimer's disease, a degenerative brain disease, bilingual patients reported showing initial symptoms of the disease an average of five years later than monolingual patients.
In a follow-up study, researchers compared the brains of bilingual and monolingual patients matched on the severity of Alzheimer's symptoms.
Surprisingly, the bilinguals' brains had more physical signs of disease than their monolingual counterparts, even though their outward behaviour and abilities were the same.
If the brain is an engine, bilingualism may help it to go farther on the same amount of fuel.
Furthermore, the benefits associated with bilingual experience seem to start very early.
In one study, researchers taught seven-month-old babies growing up in monolingual or bilingual homes that when they heard a tinkling sound, a puppet appeared on one side of a screen.
items.explain: Q38: The question asks about benefits before learning to speak — paragraph G describes a study with *'seven-month-old babies'* who cannot yet talk, but bilingual babies successfully learned a new rule. This shows advantages before speech begins. So the answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: Halfway through the study, the puppet began appearing on the opposite side of the screen.
In order to get a reward, the infants had to adjust the rule they'd learned; only the bilingual babies were able to successfully learn the new rule.

items.sentence_raw: This suggests that for very young children, as well as for older people, navigating a multilingual environment imparts advantages that transfer far beyond language.
